newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-AUSTRALIA DISCOVER NEW LEG-SPINNING ENIGMA.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-AUSTRALIA DISCOVER NEW LEG-SPINNING ENIGMA.

text.p: Australian batsman Michael Bevan this week achieved a very rare feat in the specialised world of modern test cricket.
The 26-year-old, selected three years ago as a free-swinging middle-order batsman, transformed himself into a world-class leg-spin bowler in the fourth test against West Indies.
Bevan took 10 wickets in a man-of-the-match performance in Adelaide which saw Australia retain the Frank Worrell trophy by taking an unbeatable 3-1 series lead.

His career-best six for 82 in West Indies' second innings led Australia to a crushing victory by an innings and 183 runs. Bevan's haul, hailed in Australian media on Wednesday as a "Perfect 10", also more than doubled his test wicket tally.
The win elevated Australia to the top of the unofficial Wisden Cricketers' Almanack world championship standings.
Bevan's performance was a revelation for the Australian team after they gambled in selecting him as a front-line spinner for the first time in his career.
Bevan himself struggled to believe his cricketing "Jekyll and Hyde" act, insisting he was still a batsman first and a bowler second.

"Just because I've got six wickets, my philosophy hasn't changed -- I'm still sort of a part-timer," Bevan insisted after the match. "But I'm very happy with the way I bowled and I'm on a bit of a high at the moment."
Bevan sheepishly added he was "probably going to get a bit of stick for getting it (10 wickets) before my test century".

While fast bowlers like Imran Khan of Pakistan, India's Kapil Dev and New Zealand's Sir Richard Hadlee matured into century-making test batsmen, batsmen have only rarely become dangerous bowlers later in their careers.
But Australia's blonde leg-spinning star Shane Warne now has a partner and the new leg-spin twins are set to terrorise the world's batsmen.
The combination of the right-armed Warne, all accuracy and occasionally vicious turn, and Bevan's bouncy left-armers proved irresistible in Adelaide.
The pair took 16 wickets between them to destroy the West Indian batting line-up twice, with Bevan outstanding on a flat, gentle pitch offering little help to spinners.

When bowling together, the pair delivered a right-arm, left-arm combination which dazzled the tourists. Bevan's dismissal of Shivnarine Chanderpaul, West Indies' most consistent batsman on tour, perfectly illustrated his talents.
Brought on before Warne within the first hour of West Indies' second innings, Bevan confused the pint-sized left-hander with a ball which spun the wrong way.
His next ball was a top-spinner, which Chanderpaul treated like the previous delivery and edged to a sprawling Australia captain Mark Taylor at slip.
Taylor was enthusiastic about Bevan's ability and believed even better lies ahead.
"If he keeps bowling like that and his batting gets better then he'll be something special in test cricket," an ebullient Taylor said after the win by an innings and 183 victory.
Bevan also scored an unusually hesitant 85 not out in Australia's innings of 517, lifting his test average to 34.75.

Bevan's concentration on his batting shortcomings in in post-match comments illustrated his personality. A quiet, intense man, Bevan does not the fit the mould of the modern Australian cricketer typified by the brash and confident Warne.

"He's not your Ian Botham, larrikin type of guy," Taylor said of Bevan. "He's not the guy who goes down the pub after the game and has a beer. He'll go back to the gym and work out for an hour, even after making 150."
"He's not what you'd call your normal Aussie cricketer."
Normal or not, Bevan has cemented his place in the side for the upcoming tour of South Africa and is also likely to partner Warne during the Ashes tour of England later this year.
